items.followUp: What is the difference between fundamental and derived quantities? Give one example of each.

rubric.why: Identifies that base quantities are independent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that base quantities are independent and not defined in terms of other physical quantities.

rubric.why: Explains how derived quantities are obtained.
rubric.description: Derived quantities are obtained by combining base quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that derived quantities are formed from base quantities, for example area or speed.

modelAnswer: Base quantities are independent physical quantities; they are not defined in terms of other physical quantities.
Derived quantities are obtained by combining base quantities, for example, area and speed.

items.followUp: Define nuclear physics and state what it studies.

rubric.why: Defines the field by relating it to the atom.
rubric.description: Atomic physics is the study of atoms and their properties or structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying atomic physics as the study of atoms, their structure, or their properties.

rubric.why: Defines the field by relating it to the nucleus.
rubric.description: Nuclear physics is the study of atomic nuclei and their properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying nuclear physics as the study of nuclei or their properties.

modelAnswer: Atomic physics is the branch of physics that studies atoms and their properties.
Nuclear physics is the branch of physics that studies atomic nuclei and their properties.

items.followUp: Describe how you would find the volume of a stone using a measuring cylinder.

rubric.description: Measure and record the initial volume of water in a measuring cylinder.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the initial water volume is measured in a graduated or measuring cylinder.

rubric.why: Uses water displacement to determine the solid's volume.
rubric.description: After fully immersing the solid, subtract the initial water volume from the final volume; the difference is the solid's volume.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the increase in water volume equals the volume of the solid.

modelAnswer: Pour water into a measuring cylinder and record its initial volume, V₁.
Fully immerse the irregular solid in the water and record the final volume, V₂.
Volume of the solid = V₂ − V₁.

items.followUp: Explain how you can tell whether a body is at rest or in motion relative to a reference point.

rubric.why: States the condition for rest relative to a reference point.
rubric.description: A body is at rest if its position relative to its surroundings or a reference point does not change with time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing unchanged position over time relative to a reference point.

rubric.why: States the condition for motion relative to a reference point.
rubric.description: A body is in motion if its position relative to its surroundings or a reference point changes with time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing changing position over time relative to a reference point.

modelAnswer: A body is at rest if its position relative to its surroundings or a reference point does not change with time.
A body is in motion if its position relative to its surroundings or a reference point changes with time.

items.followUp: What is random motion? Give two examples.

rubric.why: Defines the irregular or unpredictable nature of random motion.
rubric.description: Random motion is motion in which direction changes irregularly or unpredictably.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining random motion as irregular or unpredictable motion, especially with respect to direction.

rubric.why: Provides two examples of random motion.
rubric.description: Examples include gas molecules and dust particles moving in air.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving two valid examples of random motion.

modelAnswer: Random motion is motion in which an object's direction changes irregularly or unpredictably.
Examples include the motion of gas molecules and dust particles in air.

items.followUp: State one effect a force can have on a body's motion.

rubric.why: Identifies force as a push or pull.
rubric.description: A force is a push or a pull.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining force as a push or pull.

rubric.why: States the effect of a force on a body.
rubric.description: A force changes or tends to change a body's state of rest or motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that force changes or tends to change the state of rest or motion of a body.

modelAnswer: A force is a push or a pull.
It changes or tends to change the state of rest or motion of a body.

items.followUp: State Newton's Second Law of Motion.

rubric.why: States what happens to a body when no unbalanced force acts.
rubric.description: A body remains at rest or continues in uniform motion in a straight line.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both rest and uniform straight-line motion as the unchanged states.

rubric.why: Identifies the condition that changes the body's state of motion.
rubric.description: The state changes only when acted upon by an unbalanced external force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying an unbalanced external force as the cause of a change.

modelAnswer: A body remains at rest or continues to move with uniform velocity in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force.

items.followUp: Differentiate between mass and weight, including their SI units.

rubric.description: Mass is the amount or quantity of matter in a body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining mass as the amount of matter in a body.

rubric.why: Distinguishes weight from mass as a gravitational force.
rubric.description: Weight is the gravitational force acting on a body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying weight as the force of gravity on a body; unit or variation with location may also support this distinction.

modelAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter in a body; its SI unit is the kilogram (kg), and it remains constant from place to place.
Weight is the gravitational force acting on a body; its SI unit is the newton (N), and it varies with the gravitational field strength.
